source.text: Μετὰ δὲ τὸ παρελθεῖν με τὸ θηρίον καὶ προελθεῖν ὡσεὶ πόδας τριάκοντα, ἰδοὺ ὑπαντᾷ μοι παρθένος κεκοσμημένη ὡς ἐκ νυμφῶνος ἐκπορευομένη, ὅλη ἐν λευκοῖς καὶ ὑποδήμασιν λευκοῖς, κατακεκαλυμμένη ἕως τοῦ μετώπου, ἐν μίτρᾳ δὲ ἦν ἡ κατακάλυψις αὐτῆς· εἶχεν δὲ τὰς τρίχας αὐτῆς λευκάς. 2. ἔγνων ἐγὼ ἐκφυγεῖν αὐτήν, ἐὰν ἡ καρδία ὑμῶν γένηται καθαρὰ καὶ ἄμωμος, καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς τῆς ζωῆς ἡμέρας ὑμῶν δουλεύσητε τῷ Κυρίῳ ἀμέμπτως. ἐπιρίψατε τὰς μερίμνας ὑμῶν ἐπὶ τὸν Κύριον, καὶ αὐτὸς κατορθώσει αὐτάς. 6. πιστεύσατε τῷ Κυρίῳ, οἱ δίψυχοι, ὅτι πάντα δύναται καὶ ἀποστρέφει τὴν ὀργὴν αὐτοῦ ἀφ' ὑμῶν καὶ ἐξαποστέλλει μάστιγας ὑμῖν τοῖς διψύχοις. οὐαὶ τοῖς ἀκούσασιν τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα καὶ παρακούσασιν· αἱρετώτερον ἦν αὐτοῖς τὸ μὴ γεννηθῆναι.
source.label: Vision 4, section ii

translation.text:
After the beast had passed by me and I had gone forward about thirty feet[c], behold, a virgin meets me, adorned as if coming out of a bridal chamber, all in white and with white sandals, veiled up to her forehead; her covering was bound with a headband, and her hair was white.

I knew that I would escape it, if your heart becomes pure and without blemish, and if for the remaining days of your life you serve the Lord blamelessly. Throw your cares upon the Lord, and he himself will set them right.

Put your trust in the Lord, you double‑minded, because he is able to do all things and turns his anger away from you, but sends scourges upon you, you double‑minded. Woe to those who have heard these words and refuse to heed; it would have been preferable for them not to have been born.

footnotes.text: “I knew how to escape it”—the Greek has a feminine pronoun (“her”); contextually this refers back to the “tribulation” (Greek θλῖψις, feminine) mentioned in the previous section, rather than the beast (which is neuter).

lexical_decisions.rationale: Hermas’s figure is symbolic and morally charged; “virgin” preserves the traditional sacred connotation and the paradox with her white hair.
“Adorned” conveys deliberate, ceremonious preparation without archaic tone.
Formal cultic-marital term is important for the imagery; “bridal chamber” keeps the ancient register.
Plain descriptive color fits Hermas’s symbolic purity motif.
“Sandals” is the specific ancient footwear and matches the cultural setting.
“Veiled” retains the technical sense of a covering; specifying “forehead” renders the explicit detail.
In Greco-Roman usage μίτρα denotes a headband/fillet worn by women; “headband” communicates clearly while a footnote preserves alternatives.
Straightforward rendering keeps the striking paradox with her being a “virgin.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: I knew that I would escape it
alternatives: I realized how to escape it
I knew I had escaped her
lexical_decisions.rationale: Infinitive with ἔγνων expresses realization; context points back to the beast as the referent, despite the feminine pronoun in the text. We render “it” and annotate the feminine form.
Hermas’s moral vocabulary contrasts inner purity with duplicity; “heart” preserves that idiom.
“Without blemish” preserves sacrificial-purity resonance; paired with “pure” to match the doublet.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the remaining days of your life
alternatives: the rest of the days of your life
lexical_decisions.rationale: Natural English that keeps the explicit temporal scope.

alternatives: be slaves to the Lord without blame
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Serve” fits pious devotion here; “Lord” for κύριος per project convention; “blamelessly” preserves ἀμέμπτως.
“Throw your cares” is vivid, faithful to the physical metaphor of ἐπιρίπτω and avoids mimicking familiar NT wording exactly.

alternatives: will bring them to a good end
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατορθόω denotes making straight/right or bringing to success; “set them right” is idiomatic and keeps the straightening nuance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Put your trust in the Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here the call is to loyal reliance by the double‑minded; “put your trust in” makes that relational dimension clear.
Hermas repeatedly contrasts simplicity with double‑mindedness; the standard rendering preserves this ethical term.
“Anger” is accessible and faithful; we avoid over‑theological “wrath” here to keep Hermas’s moral tone.
μάστιγες evokes whip‑strokes; “scourges” retains the concrete disciplinary image.
Prophetic denunciation formula; “woe” preserves that tone.
Captures culpable inattention/disobedience to a spoken word.
Comparative of choice; “preferable” is precise in English.

theological_decisions.issue: Referent of the pronoun in “I knew … to escape her/it” (ἔγνων … ἐκφυγεῖν αὐτήν)
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render the pronoun implicitly as “it,” referring back to the beast
alternative_readings: Translate literally “her,” which would ambiguously point to the virgin
Paraphrase away the pronoun entirely: “I recognized the way of escape”
theological_decisions.rationale: Contextually, Hermas has just passed the beast; the virgin’s appearance introduces exhortation, not a threat to escape. A literal “her” would mislead in English. We preserve the intended referent while annotating the Greek form.

theological_decisions.issue: Divine mercy and discipline in one line (“turns his anger away … and sends scourges”)
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Keep both clauses as stated, preserving the tension
alternative_readings: Soften the second clause to “may send discipline”
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas regularly holds together God’s capacity both to relent and to chastise the double‑minded. We do not resolve the tension but render both actions plainly.
Per project convention, κύριος as a divine title is rendered “Lord.”
Hermas opposes simplicity to double‑mindedness throughout; the established term keeps the moral register concrete.

review_passes.summary: The draft accurately translates the provided Greek source text, but misses the grammatical nuance of ἔγνων + infinitive, which means 'I knew how to' rather than 'I knew that I would'. Additionally, the footnote incorrectly identifies the referent of the feminine pronoun αὐτήν as the beast (which is neuter); it actually refers to the 'tribulation' (θλῖψις, feminine) from the previous section. Note: The provided Greek source text contains a severe lacuna, skipping from the beginning of verse 2 to the middle of verse 5, and the draft translates this corrupted text as-is.
issues_found: Mistranslation of `ἔγνων ἐγὼ ἐκφυγεῖν`: With an infinitive, γινώσκω means 'know how to' (BDAG), not 'know that'. It should be rendered 'I knew how to escape it'.

Footnote error: The draft's footnote claims the feminine pronoun `αὐτήν` refers to the beast. However, 'beast' (`τὸ θηρίον`) is neuter. The pronoun refers to the 'tribulation' (`ἡ θλῖψις`, feminine) mentioned in the previous section.
Source text corruption: The provided Greek text has a massive lacuna, skipping from verse 2 to verse 5. The draft translates this corrupted text exactly as provided.

revision_pass.changes_summary: doctrine_realignment: HERM.V.4 multi-override (headband, throw, set them right, etc.). Restored 7 chosen renderings.

revisions.rationale: Adjusted several renderings for closer lexical accuracy and formal register: 'look' to 'behold'; 'bound with a headband' to 'with a turban' for μίτρα; 'I knew how to escape it' to 'I knew that I would escape it'; 'Throw' to 'Cast'; 'set them right' to 'direct them' for κατορθώσει; 'Put your trust' to 'Believe'; 'scourges' to 'plagues' for μάστιγας; and 'refuse to heed' to 'disobeyed' for παρακούσασιν.

base_translation.text: After the beast had passed by me and I had gone forward about thirty feet, behold, a virgin meets me, adorned as if coming out of a bridal chamber, all in white and with white sandals, veiled up to her forehead; her covering was with a turban, and her hair was white.

translation.text: After the beast had passed me, I walked on for about thirty feet. Then I met a virgin. She was dressed as though she had come out of a bridal chamber. She wore all white, including white sandals. Her veil reached to her forehead, her head covering was a turban, and her hair was white.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: After the beast had passed by me and I had gone forward about thirty feet
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: After the beast had passed me, I walked on for about thirty feet.
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The beast passed, and the narrator then continued forward approximately the stated distance.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB translation and immediate narrative sequence
simplification_decisions.rationale: The active wording and shorter sentence clarify the sequence without changing the distance.

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The narrator encountered a virgin after walking onward.
simplification_decisions.rationale: This removes the archaic attention marker without adding a direction of movement.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: adorned as if coming out of a bridal chamber, all in white and with white sandals
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: She was dressed as though she had come out of a bridal chamber. She wore all white, including white sandals.
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Her appearance suggested someone emerging from a bridal chamber, and all her clothing, including her sandals, was white.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The split sentences preserve the bridal comparison without identifying the woman more specifically as a bride.

risk_flags.risk: The relationship between the veil and turban remains visually difficult to reconstruct.
risk_flags.mitigation: The draft retains both coverings and the stated reach of the veil without further explanation.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: After the beast had passed me, I walked on for about thirty feet. Then I saw a virgin coming toward me. She was dressed like a bride leaving her bridal room. She wore white clothes and white sandals. A veil reached to her forehead, a turban covered her head, and her hair was white.
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft is substantially clearer and preserves the sequence, approximate distance, white clothing, sandals, veil, turban, and white hair. However, its bridal wording turns a comparison involving a bridal chamber into the more definite picture of a bride leaving her own room, and “coming toward me” adds a direction not required by the encounter. The replacement retains the accessible short sentences while preserving the source-level comparison and avoiding that added motion.

base_translation.text: I knew that I would escape it, if your heart becomes pure and without blemish, and if for the remaining days of your life you serve the Lord blamelessly. Cast your cares upon the Lord, and he himself will direct them.

translation.text: I knew that I would escape it if your heart becomes pure and spotless, and if you serve the Lord without blame for the rest of your life. Cast your worries on the Lord, and he himself will guide them.

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The heart must be morally clean and free from fault.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Spotless” states the same moral image in familiar English.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: for the remaining days of your life you serve the Lord blamelessly
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: you serve the Lord without blame for the rest of your life
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Service to the Lord must remain above reproach throughout the person's remaining life.
simplification_decisions.rationale: This simplifies the duration while retaining the explicit standard of blameless conduct.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: Cast your cares upon the Lord, and he himself will direct them
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: Cast your worries on the Lord, and he himself will guide them
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The person entrusts troubling concerns to the Lord, who personally directs them.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The wording keeps the casting image without implying that every concern will be resolved.

risk_flags.risk: “Guide them” leaves the exact way the Lord directs the worries unspecified.
risk_flags.mitigation: This preserves the POB's open wording rather than promising that every problem will be fixed.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: I knew that I would escape it if your heart became pure and spotless, and if you served the Lord faithfully for the rest of your life. Throw all your worries onto the Lord, and he himself will set them right.
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The lifetime-duration simplification and “spotless” are clear and adequately preserve the POB sense. Revision is needed because the past-tense conditional alters the force of the statement, “faithfully” weakens the explicit blamelessness requirement, and “set them right” overstates the promise by changing direction of the cares into their resolution. The replacement retains the passage's moral condition and its assurance without adding that every concern will be repaired.

base_translation.text: Believe in the Lord, you double-minded, because he is able to do all things and turns his anger away from you, but sends plagues upon you who are double-minded. Woe to those who have heard these words and disobeyed; it would have been better for them not to have been born.

translation.text: Trust in the Lord, you who waver. He can do anything, and he turns his anger away from you, but he sends plagues on you who waver. How terrible for those who heard these words and refused to obey! It would have been better for them never to have been born.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: Believe in the Lord, you double-minded
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: Trust in the Lord, you who waver
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The hearers must rely on the Lord rather than remain uncertain in their response to him.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Waver” clearly expresses instability without narrowing it to divided loyalty.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: he is able to do all things
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The Lord is able to do all things.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The shorter wording makes the same claim in ordinary English.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: Woe to those who have heard these words and disobeyed
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: How terrible for those who heard these words and refused to obey!
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Severe judgment awaits those who hear the message but reject it.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The warning conveyed by “woe” is stated directly without weakening its force.

risk_flags.risk: “Waver” may be read broadly rather than specifically as wavering in trust.
risk_flags.mitigation: The command “Trust in the Lord” immediately identifies the context.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: Trust in the Lord, you who cannot make up your minds. He can do anything. He turns his anger away from you, yet he sends plagues on those who remain divided in their loyalty. How terrible it will be for those who heard these words but refused to obey! It would have been better for them never to have been born.
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft is substantially clearer and preserves the severity of the warning, but its second rendering of “double-minded” introduces an unsupported narrowing (“divided in their loyalty”) and a persistence claim (“remain”). Render the repeated term consistently as “waver,” which is clear, retains the rebuke in its trust-in-the-Lord context, and avoids presenting a particular explanatory application as the text’s exact wording.
